metaDescription: Six carpet extractors from Bissell, Rug Doctor and Shark compared on suction, tank size, brush design, tools and drying for homes and rentals.
expertTake: The Bissell Big Green is the best all round pick, because its large tanks, rotating brush and both-pass cleaning fit household use. The Rug Doctor Pro Deep is the choice if you want the strongest suction. The Pet TruDeep is best for pets. If you clean a carpet only once every year or two, renting is cheaper than buying any of these.
introParagraphs: A carpet extractor sprays cleaning solution into the pile, agitates it with a brush and pulls the dirty water back up with a vacuum motor. The difference between a professional-grade machine and a consumer shampooer is mostly how much water it pulls back out, since leftover moisture sets drying time and mildew risk.

This guide explains how to judge suction, brush design, tank size and tools, and which machines suit pets, large homes or occasional use. Start with the picks above for the short list, then read the reviews below to match a machine to your floors, your household and the way you plan to clean.

products.name: Bissell Big Green Professional Carpet Cleaner XL PowerBrush

specList.label: Tank
specList.value: 1.75 gal, large clean and dirty tanks

specList.label: Formula
specList.value: Two bottles of professional deep cleaning formula

products.description:
The Bissell Big Green is the best all round pick because it brings machine-class power and a rotating brush into a package a household can own. The listing gives 12 amps of power, a 1.75 gallon tank and large clean and dirty water tanks, so you make fewer trips to the sink than with a consumer upright. Rotating DirtLifter power brushes agitate the pile while the machine sprays and extracts.

Cleaning on both the forward and backward pass is the practical design feature. Many machines only extract when you pull back, but the Big Green is designed so both passes clean, which the maker says reduces time and speeds drying. A 9 inch long reach hose and a 6 inch tough stain tool handle stairs and spot treatment. Compared with the Bissell BG10 commercial unit, it is the consumer-oriented version with a brush and tools, and compared with the Rug Doctor Mighty Pro X3 it comes with two bottles of formula and a different brush design.

Ownership is about drying and rinsing. After each job, empty the dirty tank, rinse the tanks and brush roll and let the machine air dry, or the tanks grow a sour smell. Vacuum the carpet thoroughly before extraction, since dry soil turns to mud when it meets water. The machine is heavy when full, so plan on wrestling it up a staircase.
products.bestFor: Households that want rental-style cleaning at home with fewer refills and a rotating brush.
pros: Large clean and dirty tanks mean fewer trips to the sink
Cleans on both the forward and the backward passes
Rotating DirtLifter brush agitates the carpet pile
Includes a stain tool and two bottles of cleaning formula
cons: Heavy when the tanks are full, so awkward on stairs
Priced well above a basic consumer upright shampooer
Needs thorough rinsing and drying to avoid sour odors

products.name: Rug Doctor Pro Deep Commercial Carpet Cleaner Oxy Bundle

specList.label: Indicators
specList.value: Digital lights for low solution and brush roll fault

specList.label: Handle
specList.value: Adjustable comfort grip, folds for storage

specList.label: Bundle
specList.value: 48 oz Oxy cleaner and 22 oz spot and pre-treat

products.description:
The Rug Doctor Pro Deep is the maker's most powerful carpet cleaner, and its main selling point is suction. Extraction power decides how much water stays in the carpet, which sets drying time and the risk of mildew. Two removable 1.5 gallon tanks, a built-in measuring cup and an adjustable handle that folds for storage round out a design for frequent heavy use.

Digital indicator lights warn you when it is time to refill the cleaning solution and when the brush roll is not operating correctly, a useful safeguard because a stalled brush leaves stripes. Compared with the Mighty Pro X3, it adds a higher suction claim, a digital indicator and a larger bundle that includes a spot and pre-treat, and compared with the Big Green it uses 1.5 gallon tanks, slightly smaller than the Bissell's 1.75 gallon capacity. The bundle comes with 48 ounces of Oxy cleaner and 22 ounces of pre-treat for food and oil stains.

As a commercial-leaning machine it is heavier than a consumer upright and takes space in a closet. Use the measuring cup to mix solution at the label ratio, because extra detergent leaves residue that attracts dirt. Pre-treat stains, work in slow overlapping passes and rinse tanks after use. It is the choice for large homes, rentals and anyone who cleans several rooms at once.
products.bestFor: Large homes and frequent users who want the strongest suction and indicators.
pros: Maker's most powerful machine, with a strong suction claim
Digital lights flag low solution and brush roll faults
Folding adjustable handle makes storage much easier
Bundle adds a pre-treat spray for food and oil stains
cons: Premium price compared with the other machines here
Heavy and bulky for a small apartment storage closet
1.5 gal tanks are slightly smaller than the Big Green's

products.name: Rug Doctor Mighty Pro X3 Commercial Carpet Cleaner with Oxy Pack

specList.label: Build
specList.value: Same standard as Rug Doctor rental machines (listing)

specList.label: Use
specList.value: Whole home and high traffic areas

products.description:
The Mighty Pro X3 is the Rug Doctor most people recognize from the rental aisle, offered for purchase. Its listing says it is built to the same standards as the maker's rental machines, with high-pressure deep-inject spray jets, a vibrating Triple Action brush and industrial-grade suction. The idea is one pass that sprays, scrubs and extracts.

Large capacity tanks reduce refills, though the listing gives no gallon figure. Compared with the Pro Deep, it lacks the digital indicators and has a lower suction claim, but it also costs less and still brings a vibrating brush that scrubs each fiber from several angles. Against the Big Green, the Rug Doctor uses a vibrating brush rather than a rotating one, so both agitate but differ in feel. The package includes a 48 ounce Oxy carpet solution aimed at wine, mud and similar stains.

Practical use is the same as any extractor. Vacuum first, pre-treat stains, mix solution at the ratio on the bottle and make slow passes, then a dry pass to pull up water. Empty and rinse the tanks and brush after each job. If you clean carpets once or twice a year, owning one costs more than renting, but pays back if you have pets or a rental property.
products.bestFor: Owners with pets or kids who want rental-grade results without renting each time.
pros: Built to the same standard as the maker's rental machines
Vibrating Triple Action brush scrubs fibers from several angles
Deep inject spray jets push cleaner down into the pile
Oxy cleaning solution comes included in the package
cons: No digital indicator lights, unlike the Pro Deep model
Listing does not state the tank size in gallons at all
Costs far more than a consumer upright carpet shampooer

products.name: Bissell Commercial BigGreen BG10 2 Motor Deep Cleaning Extractor

specList.label: Indicator
specList.value: Flow indicator for water and solution levels

products.description:
The BG10 is the commercial version of the Bissell extractor, aimed at cleaners and rental fleets. The listing says two motors, which in extractors of this type usually means vacuum suction and the pump or brush get separate power. A flow indicator monitors water and solution levels and tells you when to refill, and a removable clean water tank is easy to fill.

The listing is brief, and says little about brush design, tank gallons or included tools. That makes it hard to compare with the Big Green, which lists a 1.75 gallon tank, a DirtLifter brush and a stain tool. The BG10 is better treated as a pro-style workhorse that you accessorize yourself. Edge-to-edge suction is claimed, which is useful for cleaning to the baseboard.

Expect a machine built for repeated heavy use rather than for a quiet household. It is bulky, so storage and stair carrying matter. Check what is included in the box before ordering. If you want a machine with brush and tool details spelled out, the Big Green or the Rug Doctor models are easier to evaluate.
products.bestFor: Cleaners and landlords who want a commercial-class two motor extractor.
pros: Two motors give suction and the brush separate power
Flow indicator warns you when it is time to refill
Edge to edge suction reaches right up to baseboards
Large capacity tanks mean fewer trips to refill them
cons: Listing gives little detail on brush, tank size or tools
Bulky and heavy, which makes storage at home a chore
Costs more than the consumer Big Green model does here

products.name: Rug Doctor Pet TruDeep Carpet Cleaner with Pet Upholstery Tool

specList.label: Suction
specList.value: Claims 30 percent more than comparable uprights (air watts, ASTM F558)

specList.label: Spray
specList.value: Super Boost setting for heavy soil

specList.label: Use
specList.value: Carpet, stairs, upholstery, car seats, pet beds

products.description:
The Pet TruDeep is a home-oriented Rug Doctor tuned for pet households. The maker claims 30 percent more suction than comparable upright cleaners, measured in air watts at the cleaner head under ASTM F558, which matters for pulling out urine and moisture. A dual cross-action brush system pairs a patented vibrating brush with a rolling brush that cleans and grooms the pile.

A Super Boost spray setting delivers extra solution on heavily soiled and high-traffic areas, and an included pet upholstery tool traps pet hair and removes stains and odors from stairs, mattresses, car seats and pet beds. Compared with the Pro Deep and Mighty Pro X3, it is a home-focused machine rather than a commercial one. Against the Shark CarpetXpert, it leans on suction while the Shark leans on a built-in stain system.

Pet messes are where a machine earns its keep. Blot fresh urine first, use an enzyme pre-treat for odor and extract several times with clean water to remove residue. Rinse the tanks and tools after each use, and do not leave dirty water inside. For old pet stains, repeat passes rather than overwetting the carpet.
products.bestFor: Households with dogs or cats who need strong suction and a tool for upholstery.
pros: Maker claims 30% more suction than comparable uprights
Dual brush action scrubs the fibers and grooms the pile
Pet upholstery tool covers stairs, car seats and pet beds
Super Boost spray tackles heavy soil and traffic lanes
cons: Suction claim is the maker's own comparison, not independent
Lighter duty than the commercial Rug Doctor models
Old pet urine odors still need enzyme pre-treatment

specList.label: Stain system

specList.label: Tanks

specList.label: Tools

products.description:
The Shark CarpetXpert is a consumer-grade upright with an unusual feature, a built-in StainStriker spot and stain remover. The handheld extends from the machine and mixes two formulas on contact, so you do not need to carry a separate tool. It combines a high-speed brushroll, PowerSpray and suction for upright cleaning, and a dual tank system keeps clean water and formula separate from dirty water.

Three tools, a 3.5 inch reversible bristle tool, an integrated crevice tool and a 7 inch wide path tool, cover stairs and upholstery. Compared with the Rug Doctor and Bissell machines, it is lighter and easier to store, but it is not a professional unit and will do less on a deep, heavily soiled carpet. Against the Rug Doctor Pet TruDeep, it focuses on stains rather than suction.

The maker says PowerSpray penetrates deeply without oversoaking so carpets dry faster, though drying time depends on the carpet and the room. It is a good choice for an apartment or a household that wants spot treatment more than whole house cleaning. Use the provided formulas, rinse the tanks and clean the brushroll after each use.
products.bestFor: Apartments and homes that need quick stain removal on carpets and upholstery.

Dual tank system keeps clean and dirty water separate
Three tools cover stairs, crevices and upholstered furniture
Lighter and easier to store than a commercial extractor
cons: Consumer grade, so less powerful than the commercial models
Smaller tanks than the Big Green and Rug Doctor machines

buyingCriteria.criterion: Judge suction by the water left behind
buyingCriteria.explanation: Suction decides how much water stays in the carpet, which sets drying time, usually several hours, and the risk of mildew. A machine that extracts well leaves the carpet damp rather than wet. The Rug Doctor Pro Deep is the maker's most powerful, the Pet TruDeep claims 30 percent more suction than comparable uprights and the Bissell BG10 uses two motors. Do a dry pass over each area with no spray to pull more water out.

Agitation loosens soil that spray alone cannot. The Bissell Big Green uses a rotating DirtLifter brush, the Rug Doctor Mighty Pro X3 uses a vibrating Triple Action brush and the Pet TruDeep pairs a vibrating brush with a rolling brush. Rotating brushes groom the pile, and vibrating brushes scrub from different angles. Heavy brush action helps with ground-in dirt but can fray loop pile carpets, so check your carpet type.

A larger tank means fewer trips to the sink. The Big Green has a 1.75 gallon tank and the Pro Deep has two 1.5 gallon tanks. Water weighs about 8.3 pounds per gallon, so a full machine is heavy, and stairs get hard. For a small apartment, a lighter machine like the Shark CarpetXpert is easier to handle.

Too much detergent leaves residue that attracts dirt. Use the measuring cup on machines such as the Pro Deep and follow the label ratio. Oxy formulas help with stains, and pet formulas and enzyme pre-treatments help with urine. Use low-foam solutions made for extractors and not general soaps, since foam can enter the vacuum motor.

A hose and tools extend the machine to stairs, upholstery and car seats. The Big Green has a 9 inch hose and a 6 inch stain tool, the Pet TruDeep has a pet upholstery tool and the Shark has three tools and an extending StainStriker. Tool length and quality matter, since stairs are often the dirtiest area. Check what is included.

Renting a machine costs a fee per day plus solution, and quality varies. Owning pays off if you clean more than once or twice a year, have pets or manage rentals. A bought machine is also available at any time, which matters for fresh stains. Count storage space and cleaning time in the cost.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps measure electrical current, and motors drive suction and the brush. The Big Green lists 12 amps, and the BG10 lists two motors. More current generally means more power, though design affects results.
specDecoder.watchFor: Amp figures vary between sources. Treat them as a rough guide, and judge extraction by how damp the carpet is after a dry pass.

specDecoder.spec: Air watts at the cleaner head
specDecoder.meaning: Air watts combine airflow and vacuum pressure into a measure of useful suction power. The Pet TruDeep cites air watts measured under ASTM F558 at the cleaner head.
specDecoder.watchFor: The claim compares against other uprights, chosen by the maker. It is not an independent ranking.

specDecoder.meaning: The gallons of clean water and dirty water the machine holds. More capacity means fewer refills but more weight. The Big Green has 1.75 gallons and the Pro Deep has two 1.5 gallon tanks.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Mighty Pro X3 and BG10 listings give no gallon figure, so check the full spec.

specDecoder.meaning: Rotating brushes spin in one direction to groom and agitate, vibrating brushes oscillate to scrub fibers, and counter-rotating sets work from two directions. Each cleans differently.
specDecoder.watchFor: Aggressive brushing can damage some loop pile or wool carpets. Check your carpet maker's advice.

specDecoder.meaning: Hot water helps dissolve oils, but most home extractors do not heat water themselves, and tap water is used. Dwell time and the right solution matter more than temperature.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not use boiling water in the tanks, since it can damage plastic parts and some carpets. Follow the manual.

howWeEvaluated.title: Suction and extraction
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared suction claims and motor design, from the Pro Deep's most powerful rating to the BG10's two motors and the Pet TruDeep's 30 percent claim. We treated each claim as a manufacturer figure and weighted drying time as the real result.

howWeEvaluated.title: Agitation and brush design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at rotating, vibrating and dual brushes. The Big Green's DirtLifter, the Mighty Pro X3's Triple Action and the Pet TruDeep's cross-action pair ranked highest. The Shark's brushroll suits lighter soil.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tanks and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared tank size, weight and handles. The Big Green's 1.75 gallon tank and the Pro Deep's two 1.5 gallon tanks lead, and the Pro Deep's folding handle helps storage. We noted that full tanks make stairs hard.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tools and extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed hoses, stain tools and included solutions. The Big Green's hose and stain tool, the Pet TruDeep's pet tool and the Shark's three tools and StainStriker are the strongest. Bundles with Oxy solutions added value.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and value
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each machine by class. The Pro Deep and BG10 are heavy duty, the Big Green and Mighty Pro X3 are pro-grade home machines, and the Pet TruDeep and Shark are lighter. We considered whether buying beats renting.

howToChoose.intro: The real difference is how much water you pull back out.

cards.label: Pro grade
cards.text: The Bissell Big Green, Rug Doctor Pro Deep, Mighty Pro X3 and BG10 are built around bigger motors, larger tanks and stronger brushes. They suit deep cleaning of heavily soiled carpet and clean several rooms per session.

cards.label: Consumer upright
cards.text: The Shark CarpetXpert and Rug Doctor Pet TruDeep are lighter and easier to store. They handle regular upkeep and stains but work harder on deep soil and large areas.

howToChoose.note: Choose pro grade for big, heavily soiled areas and annual deep cleans. Choose a consumer unit for apartments and spot work.

howToChoose.intro: A machine that is hard to move gets used less.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Pet messes need strong suction, a pet upholstery tool and a pre-treat that breaks down urine. Use an enzyme cleaner, avoid heat that sets protein stains and extract several times with clean water.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Rug Doctor Pet TruDeep is the best fit because of its suction claim and pet upholstery tool, and the Pro Deep bundle adds a spot and pre-treat for deep stains. The Bissell Big Green also suits pet owners who clean whole rooms.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you clean carpets several times a year, have pets or manage rentals. The Rug Doctor Pro Deep and Bissell Big Green extract more water, which means faster drying and fewer re-cleans.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you clean once a year or only treat spots. Rent a machine or choose the Shark CarpetXpert, since a premium extractor would sit in a closet.

maintenance.why: Dirty water left in a tank turns sour and smells. Rinse and leave the tanks open to dry.
Hair and fiber wind around the brush and cut agitation. Cut them away and rinse the brush.
Detergent residue can clog nozzles. Run clean water through the lines.

maintenance.task: Check the filter and vacuum path
maintenance.why: Foam or debris in the suction path lowers extraction. Clear it and wipe the float screen.
A cracked seal loses suction. Replace worn gaskets and hoses.
A closed wet tank grows mildew. Let everything air dry before storage.

faq.q: Is it worth buying a professional-grade carpet cleaner?
faq.a: If you clean carpets more than once or twice a year, have pets or manage rentals, yes. Owning also lets you treat fresh stains at once. For a single annual clean, renting is cheaper.

faq.q: How long do carpets take to dry?
faq.a: Drying time depends on extraction, humidity and airflow, and is commonly several hours. A dry pass with no spray pulls out more water. Run fans and keep windows open to speed drying.

faq.q: Can I use any solution in an extractor?
faq.a: Use low-foam solutions made for extractors. Excess foam can enter the vacuum motor and damage it. Follow the label ratio and the measuring cup if one is provided.

faq.q: Do Rug Doctor and Bissell machines differ much?
faq.a: Both are pro-style extractors. The Big Green uses a rotating DirtLifter brush and 1.75 gallon tanks, while the Rug Doctor models use vibrating brushes and different tank sizes. The practical gap is in handling, tools and tank size.

faq.q: Can I use a carpet cleaner on upholstery?
faq.a: Yes with the right tool. The Pet TruDeep includes a pet upholstery tool and the Shark has three tools. Check the fabric care label first and test a hidden spot.

faq.q: Will a carpet cleaner remove pet odor?
faq.a: It helps if you also use an enzyme pre-treat that breaks down urine. Blot fresh stains first and extract several times with clean water. Old stains may need repeat treatments.
